area.title: Address book list, view and delete
area.scope: The address book list (heading, intro, category tabs, search and type filter, table columns, pagination, results count, success banners), viewing one address, deleting an address (confirmation, soft delete, tombstones), organisation scoping and caller identity, and the list, read and delete APIs. Stops at adding and editing an address (address-book-add-and-edit).

sources.role: the owner's decisions: outranks every other source. It sets how the rest are weighed: the prototype wins by default over what the real services do today; only a DR1 judgement on the same difference, or a real constraint the prototype cannot express (persistence, validation, authentication, cross-service behaviour), overrides it.

claims.statement: The prototype (Design Release 2.1) wins by default over what the real services do today.

claims.statement: A DR1 judgement on the same difference overrides the prototype default.
claims.quote: Only a DR1 judgement or a real constraint the prototype can't express (persistence, validation, auth, cross-service behaviour) overrides it.

claims.statement: A real constraint the prototype cannot express overrides the prototype default; the ruling names persistence, validation, authentication and cross-service behaviour as such constraints.
claims.quote: a real constraint the prototype can't express (persistence, validation, auth, cross-service behaviour) overrides it.
claims.note: New. The quote says 'auth'; claim 6 reads it as authentication. Claim 6 adds 'such as', making the list examples; the quote's parenthesis can be read either as examples or as the full list.

claims.statement: Nothing other than a DR1 judgement on the same difference or a real constraint the prototype cannot express overrides the prototype.
claims.quote: Only a DR1 judgement or a real constraint the prototype can't express (persistence, validation, auth, cross-service behaviour) overrides it.
claims.note: New. In particular, what a real service does today is not on its own a reason to depart from the prototype.

claims.statement: Questions for people are kept to a minimum.
claims.quote: Decisions: keep questions for people to a minimum.
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: A question for people is raised only when a difference is truly exceptional and neither the prototype default nor a DR1 judgement settles it.
claims.quote: Raise one only when a difference is truly exceptional and neither the default nor DR1 settles it.
claims.note: New. Both conditions must hold. 'The default' is read as the prototype-wins default from the Precedence paragraph.

claims.statement: Increments are grouped into themes, and the themes are drawn from the evidence.
claims.quote: Themes: group the increments into themes based on the evidence.
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: Each theme's boundary is set by the code it touches.
claims.quote: Draw the boundaries by the code each one touches
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: Themes can be built in parallel on separate machines without pull requests that conflict with each other.
claims.quote: so themes can be built in parallel on separate machines without conflicting PRs.
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: The ruling's DR1 paragraph has an elision marked [...]: what the omitted words said about the DR1 parity backlog is not recorded.
The ruling does not say what makes a difference 'truly exceptional', so when a question for people is warranted is left open.

The ruling limits DR1 use to clashes between 'the real frontend' and the prototype; it does not say which frontend that is, or whether DR1 judgements apply to differences in the INS frontend, the backends or other repos.
The ruling does not say which override wins when a DR1 judgement and a real constraint the prototype cannot express point different ways on the same difference.
The ruling does not say what a real service does where a real constraint overrides the prototype: whether it keeps today's behaviour or matches the prototype as closely as the constraint allows.
The ruling does not say whether a feature or behaviour a real service has that Design Release 2.1 does not show at all counts as a difference to remove, or is left alone.
The ruling does not say what to do where the code two themes need to touch overlaps, so no boundary keeps their pull requests from conflicting.

claims.statement: Fetching one address by id returns 200 with the address, including a soft-deleted one.
claims.quote: Fetches one address by id within the caller's organisation scope, tombstones included.

claims.statement: A live address fetched by id returns every mapped field (id, name, addressLine1, townOrCity, postcode, countryCode, phone, email, organisationId, createdAt, modifiedAt) with deleted false.
A soft-deleted address fetched by id returns 200 with deleted true, so the caller can detect that it was deleted.
claims.quote:
A DELETED
   * address is returned with 200 and {@code deleted: true} so the caller can detect a deletion

claims.statement: Fetching an unknown id returns 404 as a not-found problem (type .../not-found, title 'Resource Not Found', status 404) with no errors map.
Fetching an id that belongs to another organisation returns the same 404 as an unknown id, so the existence of another organisation's address is never disclosed.
claims.quote:
An id outside the caller's
   * organisation is indistinguishable from an unknown id: both are empty, so 404 leaks no existence
   * across organisations (cv-010).
claims.note: The byte-identical cross-organisation 404 test (AddressScopingIT) is part 4's.

claims.statement: A 404 from the service is not a deletion signal: only a 200 with deleted true means the user deleted the address.
claims.quote: A 404 is therefore NOT a deletion signal: only the tombstone is.

claims.statement: Outside prod, a 404 for an address id can also mean the address has expired and been removed.
claims.quote: Outside prod it can also mean the address has expired (see below).

claims.statement: The documented get-one responses are 200, 404 (unknown id or an id outside the caller's organisation) and 500; no 400 is documented for it.
claims.quote:
'200':
          description: The address (deleted false or true) ... '404':
          description: Unknown id, or an id outside the caller's organisation scope
claims.note: Every other operation documents a 400 for a missing org header; GET by id does not, although the header filter applies to it too.

claims.statement: Delete is a soft delete: the address is not removed, its internal status flips to DELETED and modifiedAt is bumped.
claims.quote:
`DELETE /organisation/{orgId}/addresses/{operator-id}` is a **soft delete**: the document stays in MongoDB,
its internal `status` flips to `DELETED`, and `modifiedAt` is bumped.

claims.statement: A successful delete returns 204 No Content.
Deleting keeps the address's createdAt unchanged and moves modifiedAt later.
The service keeps deleted addresses as tombstones so a consumer can tell 'deleted' (200 with deleted true) from 'unknown or not yours' (404); a hard delete would make deletion undetectable.
claims.quote:
The tombstone stays fetchable by id so a consumer can tell "deleted" (200 +
   * DELETED) from "unknown or not yours" (404); a hard delete would collapse both into a 404 and
   * make deletion undetectable.

claims.statement: After a delete, the address no longer appears in the list, but fetching it by id still returns 200 with deleted true.
Deleting an already-deleted address is idempotent: it returns 204, nothing is saved again and modifiedAt is not bumped a second time.
claims.quote:
Idempotent: deleting an address that is already a tombstone is a no-op — no re-save, so
   * {@code modifiedAt} is not bumped a second time and the state is unchanged.

claims.statement: Deleting an unknown id returns a 404 not-found problem.
Deleting another organisation's address returns 404 and leaves that address active, whether the caller uses their own organisation in the path or mismatches the path and header.
In the user interface, delete is reached only through a delete-confirmation page.
claims.quote:
The
   * UI reaches this only via the delete-confirmation page.
claims.note: Stated by the backend about its consumer; the confirmation page itself is in the frontend.

claims.statement: The documented delete responses are 204, 400 (missing org header), 404 (unknown id or another organisation's id) and 500; no 409 is documented for delete.
claims.quote:
'204':
          description: Soft-deleted (or already deleted — idempotent)
        '400':
          description: Missing org header

claims.statement: A delete that collides with a concurrent change would surface as a 409 conflict problem, because delete saves through the same versioned store and the conflict handler is global, but the contract does not document a 409 for delete.
claims.note: Inferred from the code paths; no test exercises a concurrent delete through the API.

claims.statement: The service has no operation to restore (undelete) a soft-deleted address, and update refuses a tombstone, so a deletion cannot be reversed through the API.
claims.note: Looked in the controller, service and both OpenAPI documents: no restore path exists. Recorded so the reconciler can weigh whether one is needed.
